level1.text: A ball is released from rest, and air resistance is ignored. What is the speed of the ball when $3.0\,\text{s}$ have passed since the start of the fall?
An apple comes off a branch and falls from rest to the ground in $0.80\,\text{s}$. Air resistance is ignored. What is the speed of the apple when it hits the ground?

On the surface of the Moon the acceleration of free fall is $1.62\,\text{m/s}^2$. An astronaut drops a stone, which falls from rest for $4.0\,\text{s}$. What is the speed of the stone after this time?
The $(t, v)$ graph of a freely falling object is a straight line through the points $(0\,\text{s};\, 0\,\text{m/s})$ and $(5.0\,\text{s};\, 49\,\text{m/s})$. What is the acceleration of free fall?
On Mars the acceleration of free fall is $3.71\,\text{m/s}^2$. An object falls on Mars from rest for $6.0\,\text{s}$ without air resistance. What is the speed of the object?
An astronaut drops a hammer and a feather from rest at the same time from the same height on the surface of the Moon. The Moon has no atmosphere. What happens?
level1.answer: The hammer and the feather hit the ground at the same time.

choices.text: The hammer and the feather hit the ground at the same time.
choices.feedback: Correct: when there is no air resistance, all objects have the same acceleration of free fall regardless of mass. The speed of both is $v = g\,t$, so they fall equally fast.

choices.text: The hammer hits the ground first, because it is heavier.
choices.feedback: A heavier object does not fall faster. Everyday experience seems to show otherwise only because air slows a light, wide object the most, and the Moon has no air.

choices.text: The feather hits the ground first, because it is lighter.
choices.feedback: Mass does not affect the acceleration of free fall. A light object would fall more slowly only in air, and the Moon has no air to slow it down.

choices.text: Neither falls, because the Moon has no air.
choices.feedback: On the surface of the Moon the acceleration of free fall is $1.62\,\text{m/s}^2$ regardless of air, so the objects fall. The lack of air only removes air resistance.

level1.text: The $(t, v)$ graph of a freely falling object is a straight line through the origin with a slope of $9.8\,\text{m/s}^2$. What does the slope tell us?
level1.answer: The speed increases by $9.8\,\text{m/s}$ every second.

choices.text: The speed increases by $9.8\,\text{m/s}$ every second.
choices.feedback: Correct: the slope $\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$ tells how much the speed changes per unit of time. The unit $\text{m/s}^2$ means $\text{m/s}$ per second.

choices.text: The speed of the object is $9.8\,\text{m/s}$ all the time.
choices.feedback: The speed is not constant but increases: it is given by $v = g\,t$. The number $9.8\,\text{m/s}^2$ is the size of the increase in speed per second, not the speed itself.

choices.text: The object falls $9.8\,\text{m}$ farther every second.
choices.feedback: The unit of the slope is $\text{m/s}^2$, not metres. It tells the change in speed, not the distance travelled. The distance grows by more and more each second, because the speed increases.

choices.text: The speed of the object is $9.8\,\text{m/s}$ only after one second, and before that it is zero.
choices.feedback: The speed increases steadily right from the start of the fall, so it is, for example, $4.9\,\text{m/s}$ after half a second. The line starts from the origin.

level1.text: On the surface of the Earth the acceleration of free fall is $9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$. So the speed of a freely falling object increases by $9.81\,\text{m/s}$ every second. By how many $\text{km/h}$ does the speed increase every second?

level2.text: A ball is released from rest and hits the ground at a speed of $12.0\,\text{m/s}$. Air resistance is ignored. How long did the ball fall?

The figure shows the $(t, v)$ graphs of bodies dropped from rest on two planets without an atmosphere. After how many seconds from the drop does the body on planet B have the same speed that the body on planet A has $5.0\,\text{s}$ after the drop?
The speed of a falling object is $12.0\,\text{m/s}$ at some moment, and there is no air resistance. How large is the speed $1.50\,\text{s}$ later?

The speed of a freely falling object is measured at two moments: $9.7\,\text{m/s}$ at the moment $t = 1.0\,\text{s}$ and $29.3\,\text{m/s}$ at the moment $t = 3.0\,\text{s}$. Calculate the acceleration of free fall from these measurements.

In a light gate measurement the speed $v$ of a small object was measured at different moments $t$ from the start of the fall, when the object was released from rest. Draw the $(t, v)$ graph from the measurement points, fit a straight line to the points and determine its slope. What is the acceleration of free fall $g$ according to the measurement? Compare the result with the table value $9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$.

level2.text:
An object was released from rest, but the measurement was started only at the moment $t = 0$, when the object had already fallen for a while. The speed was measured at different moments.

Draw the $(t, v)$ graph from the measurement points and fit a straight line to the points. The line does not pass through the origin. How many seconds before the start of the measurement was the object released? Explain what the intercept of the line with the $v$ axis tells.

data.caption: Speed of a falling object from the start of the measurement

level2.text:
Students measure the acceleration of free fall with two light gates placed one below the other vertically. The speed of an object $5.0\,\text{cm}$ long, dropped from rest, is obtained at each gate from the length of the object and the time $\Delta t_\text{light}$ for which the light is blocked.

The moment of the drop is not known accurately, but a clock measures the moments $t$ when the blocking of the light is halfway in time. At that moment the speed of the object equals its average speed during the blocking.

Calculate the acceleration of free fall from the measurements in the table. Explain why $g$ can be obtained from the speeds at the two gates even though the moment of the drop is not known.

In a vacuum chamber two balls of the same size are dropped from rest from the same height at the same time: the mass of the heavier one is $4.0\,\text{kg}$ and that of the lighter one $1.0\,\text{kg}$. The speed of the heavier ball $2.0\,\text{s}$ after the drop is $19.6\,\text{m/s}$. What is the speed of the lighter ball at the same moment?

choices.feedback: This assumes that speed is proportional to mass, so a ball four times lighter would be four times slower. In free fall the speed $v = g\,t$ does not depend on mass.
Here the number $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$ has been read as a speed. It tells how much the speed grows each second, and the speed after two seconds is $g\,t$.
Correct: there is no air resistance, so both balls are in free fall and the speed is $v = g\,t$ regardless of mass.

This assumes that the light ball accelerates four times as much because it is four times lighter. Mass does not affect the acceleration of free fall, so the speed is the same as that of the heavier ball.

reasons.text: The balls are of the same size and they start from rest.
reasons.feedback: The statement is true, but it does not explain the answer. Objects of different sizes would also fall equally fast in a vacuum, and starting from rest only tells that $v = g\,t$ begins from zero.

reasons.text: The heavier ball is pulled harder towards the Earth, so its speed grows faster.
reasons.feedback: This is a common misconception. The Earth does pull the heavier ball harder, but the heavier ball is also harder to set in motion, and these two effects cancel each other. The acceleration of free fall $g$ is the same for all objects.

reasons.text: The acceleration of free fall $g$ is the same for all objects without air resistance, so the speed $v = g\,t$ does not depend on mass.
reasons.feedback: Correct: the speed grows by the same amount every second, $g$, regardless of mass, so the balls are equally fast at every moment.

reasons.text: The lighter ball is easier to set in motion, so its speed grows faster.
reasons.feedback: It is true that a lighter object is easier to set in motion, but in free fall it is also pulled less. The overall effect cancels, and the acceleration is the same $g$.

level3.text: In a vacuum chamber two balls with masses $0.50\,\text{kg}$ and $4.0\,\text{kg}$ are dropped from rest at the same time. How many times as large is the speed of the heavier ball as the speed of the lighter ball when $1.5\,\text{s}$ have passed since the start of the fall?

An unknown planet has no atmosphere. There the speed of a stone dropped from rest is $14.8\,\text{m/s}$ after $4.0\,\text{s}$. After how many seconds from the start of the fall is the speed of the stone $30.0\,\text{m/s}$?

A ball is dropped from rest in air, and its speed is measured to be $25.0\,\text{m/s}$ after $3.00\,\text{s}$. By how many $\text{m/s}$ is the speed smaller than the speed the ball would have in free fall without air resistance?

The speeds of two objects, a small ball and a coffee filter paper, were measured from a video at moments $t$ from the start of the fall. The objects were released from rest in air.

Draw the $(t, v)$ graphs of both in the same coordinate system. At what point, and why, does the model $v = g\,t$ stop being valid for the filter paper but not yet for the ball? By what percentage is the speed of the filter paper smaller than the speed given by the model at the moment $0.40\,\text{s}$?

data.caption: Speed of the ball and the filter paper in air

level3.text:
A student dropped an object from rest and measured its speed at three clock readings $t$. The clock had been running already before the drop, but the student did not know for how long.

For each row the student calculated the quotient $\dfrac{v}{t}$ and got the values $7.5\,\text{m/s}^2$, $8.9\,\text{m/s}^2$ and $9.2\,\text{m/s}^2$. However, the acceleration of free fall is constant.

Explain why the quotients differ from each other and why they are too small. Calculate $g$ in another way so that the zero point of the clock does not affect the result, and justify the method. How many seconds before the drop had the clock been started?

data.caption: Speed of a falling object at clock readings
